issues.legal_issue: A consolidation authority cannot modify or cancel proprietary rights conveyed by a permanent Sanad granted in lieu of compensation.
material_facts: The appellant had been allotted land and placed in possession before the Central Government permanently transferred ownership to her by Sanad.
The consolidation authority later took part of the appellant’s land and allotted it to another allottee.
The appellant challenged the consolidation authority’s power to disturb the ownership rights conveyed by the Sanad.
issues.conclusion: The consolidation authorities had no jurisdiction or power to modify or cancel the proprietary rights granted by the Sanad.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 permits the Central Government to transfer property to a displaced person in payment of compensation. Such a permanent transfer conveys proprietary rights, and the Sanad could be cancelled only by the authority that granted it.

predicates.consolidation_proceeding: The dispute arises from proceedings in which an authority rearranges land holdings for consolidation.
predicates.permanent_compensation_sanad_granted: The government permanently conveyed proprietary rights in land to a displaced person in lieu of compensation by a formal grant.
predicates.consolidation_authority_reallocated_sana: A consolidation authority took or reassigned land covered by that grant.
predicates.consolidation_authority_lacks_power_to_m: The consolidation authority lacks power to alter or cancel the proprietary rights conveyed by the grant.

issues.definition: When a consolidation proceeding involves land permanently conveyed by government in lieu of compensation and the consolidation authority reassigns that land, the authority lacks power to alter or cancel the rights conveyed.

issues.legal_issue: The restriction on transfers during consolidation proceedings does not apply to a government conveyance of a Sanad in lieu of compensation.
material_facts: The Sanad permanently transferred the Central Government’s rights in the land to the appellant in lieu of compensation.
The respondent argued that the transfer was prohibited because consolidation proceedings were underway.
The transfer was made by the Central Government under the displaced persons compensation scheme, rather than by a landowner or tenant transferring a holding.
issues.conclusion: The transfer-of-property restriction in the consolidation legislation did not apply to the transfer of the Sanad.
issues.legal_principle: Section 30 of the East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948 concerns transfers or dealings by a landowner or tenant during consolidation proceedings. A transfer of rights by the Central Government under Section 10 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, in lieu of compensation, is of a different character and is not within Section 30.

predicates.consolidation_proceeding: The dispute concerns a transfer made while land consolidation proceedings are underway.
predicates.government_conveyance_in_lieu_of_compens: The government conveyed property rights to a displaced person in payment of compensation.
predicates.conveyance_made_by_sanad: The government made the conveyance through a formal Sanad.
predicates.consolidation_transfer_restriction_does_: The restriction on transfers during consolidation proceedings does not apply to the government’s conveyance by Sanad.

issues.definition: When government conveys property rights in lieu of compensation by Sanad during consolidation proceedings, the consolidation transfer restriction does not apply to that conveyance.

issues.legal_issue: A writ petition dismissed in limine without a decision on the merits does not bar a later suit by res judicata.
material_facts: The appellant challenged a consolidation order in a writ petition.
The High Court dismissed that petition in limine by a one-word order, without deciding the merits of the issues.
The appellant later brought a suit challenging the consolidation authority’s power, and the lower courts treated the earlier dismissal as barring the suit.
issues.conclusion: The summary dismissal of the earlier writ petition did not operate as res judicata, so the suit was not barred on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure embodies the rule of res judicata. As explained in Workmen of Cochin Port Trust v. Board of Trustees of the Cochin Port Trust, a matter decided on the merits by a speaking order in a writ petition may operate as res judicata, but a dismissal in limine or a dismissal on grounds such as laches or an available alternative remedy does not bar another remedy on that basis.

rule.if: civil_suit_after_writ and (writ_dismissed_in_limine or writ_dismissed_for_laches or writ_dismissed_for_alternative_remedy) and not writ_issue_decided_on_merits_by_speaking_order

predicates.civil_suit_after_writ: A person brings a civil suit after previously seeking relief in a writ petition concerning the dispute.
predicates.writ_dismissed_in_limine: The court dismissed the writ petition at the threshold without deciding the issues on their merits.
predicates.writ_dismissed_for_laches: The court dismissed the writ petition because of delay.
predicates.writ_dismissed_for_alternative_remedy: The court dismissed the writ petition because another remedy was available.
predicates.writ_issue_decided_on_merits_by_speaking: The court gave a reasoned order deciding the issue on its merits in the writ petition.
predicates.earlier_writ_dismissal_does_not_bar_suit: The earlier writ dismissal does not prevent the later suit from proceeding on the ground of res judicata.

issues.definition: When a civil suit follows a writ petition dismissed in limine, for delay, or because another remedy was available, and the issue was not decided on its merits by a reasoned order, the earlier dismissal does not bar the suit by res judicata.
